record.name: Choose a DNA sequence model for genomic element annotation
record.description: Which DNA sequence model, and which way of using it, classifies genomic elements such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and histone marks most accurately for my sequences?

attributes.question: Which DNA sequence model, and which way of using it, classifies genomic elements such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and histone marks most accurately for my sequences?
intended_users: Researchers choosing a DNA sequence model to annotate or classify regions of a genome
Method developers comparing a new DNA sequence model with published ones
attributes.decision: Choose a DNA language model, and whether to probe its frozen embeddings or fine-tune it, for a sequence annotation task.
inputs: DNA sequences of the element type of interest, with genome build and species
Labelled examples, or none if only a frozen probe is planned
A compute budget, which decides whether fine-tuning is possible
attributes.output: Per-task scores for each model under each training regime, with the task's split, kept separate by benchmark.
attributes.setting: Research genome annotation from sequence. Short-range and long-range tasks, frozen probes and fine-tuning are separate comparisons; a rank on one does not transfer to another.
exclusions: Variant effect prediction, which has its own use cases for missense, regulatory, rare-disease and splicing variants
Sequence conservation scores and synthetic promoter expression level, which are not element annotation
Pooling scores across benchmarks: each runs its own models, splits and probes
Gene expression level, three-dimensional genome structure, and classifying a sequence's species or viral lineage, which answer other questions
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from four studies: GenBench, SegmentNT, the Nucleotide Transformer benchmark and GUANinE v1.1. GUANinE contributes only two regression tasks. The models they cover overlap only partly, so a model ranked well in one may be missing from the others.

Simple comparators are in the evidence (GUANinE's 5-mer and GC-content baselines, GenBench's CNN, a raw-sequence probe in the Nucleotide Transformer benchmark), but none has been named as the baseline these models must beat.
GENEB's results are not used yet: each model's score mixes element categories with species and virus classification and with averages over all tasks, and the categories have to be separated first.

BEND, DART-Eval and Gene-MTEB results cannot be used yet: their scored results have not passed review or are recorded in a form that cannot be linked. BEND's reviewed tests are variant effect tasks, which this page excludes.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review, and nothing here was reproduced.

record.name: Predict glycan properties from structure
record.description: Which model predicts a glycan's taxonomy, immunogenicity or glycosylation type from its structure?

attributes.question: Which model predicts a glycan's taxonomy, immunogenicity or glycosylation type from its structure?
intended_users: Glycobiologists choosing a model to annotate or screen glycan structures
Method developers comparing glycan representation models
attributes.decision: Choose a model for predicting a glycan property from its structure.
inputs: Glycan structures in a machine-readable form
Labels for the property, which decide which tasks apply
attributes.output: Per-task accuracy and macro-F1 for each model on the same splits.
attributes.setting: Research glycobiology. Taxonomic prediction, immunogenicity and glycosylation type are separate tasks and are not pooled.
exclusions: Glycan-protein interaction prediction, which these tasks do not measure
Any clinical or immunological conclusion from an immunogenicity score
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from one study, the GlycanGT paper's Supplementary Table S4, which compares GlycanGT with four graph baselines (GlycanAA, Graphormer, RGCN, SweetNet) on the GlycanML tasks. It is the GlycanGT developers' own table, and on class accuracy GlycanAA scores above GlycanGT (0.746 against 0.694). One study cannot settle the question.
GlycanML's own published results cannot be linked yet, because they name methods rather than the exact versions run.
Most results carry a standard deviation over three seeds.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Judge the quality of generated protein backbones
record.description: Which generative model produces protein backbones that are designable, diverse and unlike known structures?

attributes.question: Which generative model produces protein backbones that are designable, diverse and unlike known structures?
intended_users: Protein designers choosing a generative model for unconditional backbone generation
Method developers comparing generative protein models
attributes.decision: Choose a generative model for producing backbones to take forward to sequence design and testing.
inputs: The length range of the backbones wanted
How many designs can be generated and screened computationally
attributes.output: Designability, diversity and novelty of generated backbones at each length, measured in silico.
attributes.setting: Research protein design, unconditional generation with no target. Every measure here is computational; none says a design will fold or function when made.
exclusions: Designing a binder to a chosen target, which has its own use case
Any claim that a generated backbone will express, fold or function: nothing here is made or tested
Sequence design and inverse folding
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from one study, the Genie 3 paper's Table 3, which compares 13 method and version rows at short monomer lengths. It is the developer's own table, and 11 of the 13 rows are versions not linked to a model, so only two models can be compared.

Scaffold-Lab's unconditional generation results, the second study this question needs, are held until one of its sources clears review. ProteinBench's generation tracks are recorded in a form that cannot be linked yet.
Designability is measured by self-consistency through a structure predictor, so a model that matches the predictor's biases scores well. No experimental outcome is linked.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Annotate protein function from sequence
record.description: Which method predicts the functions of protein sequences, such as Gene Ontology terms or enzyme classes, most accurately on held-out proteins?

attributes.question: Which method predicts the functions of protein sequences, such as Gene Ontology terms or enzyme classes, most accurately on held-out proteins?
intended_users: Researchers annotating proteins from a new genome, metagenome or design campaign
attributes.decision: Choose a function prediction method, and decide whether its accuracy is enough to annotate without manual curation.
inputs: Whether close homologues with known function exist, which sets what a sequence-similarity baseline would achieve
attributes.output: Accuracy of each method on held-out proteins, separately for molecular function, biological process, cellular component and enzyme class.
attributes.setting: Research protein annotation. Prospective evaluation, where proteins are annotated after the predictions were submitted, is stronger evidence than a fixed held-out split and is kept apart from it.
exclusions: Predicting the effect of mutations on function, which has its own use cases
Structure prediction, and function inferred from a predicted structure without a scored evaluation
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from one study, the HyPLM technical report, run by the developer of one of the compared models. It probes frozen protein language model embeddings on Gene Ontology and enzyme-class tasks with fixed splits. One study cannot settle the question.

The splits do not state a sequence identity cut between training and test proteins, so these results do not say how a method does on proteins with no close annotated relative. The DGEB enzyme-class test set is 128 proteins.
CAFA3's prospective evaluation, where proteins are annotated after predictions are submitted, has not passed review; it is the stronger evidence for this question once reviewed.
No baseline, such as transferring the annotation of the nearest sequence match, has been named.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Choose a protein language model representation for property prediction
record.description: Which protein language model's representation gives the best predictions of a measured protein property when a probe is trained on its embeddings?

attributes.question: Which protein language model's representation gives the best predictions of a measured protein property when a probe is trained on its embeddings?
intended_users: Protein engineers choosing an embedding to train a property predictor on
Method developers comparing protein language models as feature extractors
attributes.decision: Choose a protein language model to embed sequences with, and a probe to train on those embeddings, for a measured property.
inputs: Protein sequences and measured labels for the property
A split that reflects how the predictor will be used, such as holding out high-mutation or unseen-target sequences
A compute budget for embedding and probing
attributes.output: Per-task scores for each model's frozen representation under the same probe and split.
attributes.setting: Research protein engineering and annotation. Frozen-representation probing only: a score here does not say how a model would do fine-tuned.
exclusions: Zero-shot variant effect scoring from a model's likelihood, which is the protein variant effect use case
Function annotation against an ontology, which has its own use case
Folding stability of substitutions as an endpoint on its own, which is the protein stability use case; whole-protein melting temperature is kept, as a measured property of the protein
Pretraining perplexity and likelihood, which measure the model's fit to sequences rather than a property
Embedding throughput and other resource measures, which are a cost rather than a property score
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence on the board comes from one study, the HyPLM technical report, by the developer of one of the compared models. It ran HyPLM-Flash and 28 public checkpoints from 13 families; 12 of the systems it reports are compared on the tasks linked here. One study cannot settle the question.

A Rewire run on one rhodopsin wavelength split found an amino-acid composition baseline (Spearman 0.42) ahead of frozen ESM-2 probes (Spearman -0.22 and -0.15). Each system in that run is recorded on its own, so the board does not compare them.
FLIP and PFMBench results are recorded in a form that cannot be linked yet, TAPE's have not passed review, and the DeepProtein benchmark's are held until one of its sources clears review.
Each task is one split of one dataset.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Predict RNA structure to guide an experiment
record.description: Which method predicts an RNA's three-dimensional structure reliably enough to plan an experiment on it?

attributes.question: Which method predicts an RNA's three-dimensional structure reliably enough to plan an experiment on it?
intended_users: Structural biologists choosing an RNA structure predictor
Researchers designing mutations, probes or constructs from a predicted RNA fold
attributes.decision: Choose an RNA structure predictor, and judge how far to trust its model for a given RNA.
inputs: An RNA sequence, and its partners if it forms a complex
Whether similar structures were released before the method's training cut-off
attributes.output: Accuracy of predicted structures on targets the methods had not seen, separately for easy and hard sets and for monomers and complexes.
attributes.setting: Research RNA structural biology. Monomers, RNA-RNA complexes and RNA-protein complexes are separate comparisons, as are easy and hard sets.
exclusions: Inverse folding and RNA sequence design
Secondary structure read from a language model's attention map, which measures what the model learned rather than a usable structure
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from two studies. The independent benchmark of Ludaic and Elofsson 2026 tests ten methods on structures released after their training cut-offs. The RhoFold+ developers' table covers six CASP15 targets, each scored on the best of five predictions picked against the true structure.
The ordering of AlphaFold 3 and RhoFold+ rests on the RhoFold+ developers' table. Without it no model is compared in two studies.
No test measures whether a method's confidence tells a good prediction from a bad one, so how far to trust one model for one RNA is not answered here.
Easy and hard sets are kept apart, except the two interface tests (RNA-RNA and RNA-protein), which pool both.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Integrate single-cell datasets and correct batch effects
record.description: Which method combines single-cell datasets from different batches, laboratories or technologies while keeping the biological differences between cells?

attributes.question: Which method combines single-cell datasets from different batches, laboratories or technologies while keeping the biological differences between cells?
intended_users: Single-cell analysts combining datasets into one atlas or reference
Method developers comparing integration methods or pretrained embeddings
attributes.decision: Choose an integration method or a pretrained embedding for combining single-cell datasets.
inputs: Count matrices from several batches, with batch labels and cell-type labels where known
Whether an embedding may be trained on the data or must stay frozen
attributes.output: Batch-correction and biological-conservation scores for each method on the same datasets, and the trade-off between the two.
attributes.setting: Research single-cell analysis. Batch removal and conservation of biology pull against each other, so they are reported separately and never summed into one verdict without saying how.
exclusions: Transferring cell-type labels to a new dataset, which has its own use case
Clustering agreement or embedding separation presented as correct cell identity
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from two studies: the HyCell technical report, which scores frozen embeddings of eleven pretrained models and PCA on seven held-out atlases, and Kedzierska et al. 2025, which scores zero-shot embeddings of single-cell foundation models beside Harmony, scVI and highly variable gene selection. HyCell is the developer's own evaluation.
Both studies score embeddings with scIB metrics; neither runs the methods on a user's own batches end to end.
scIB's own published comparison has not passed review, and SCMBench's RNA-ATAC integration is held until one of its sources clears review.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

record.name: Classify viral and microbial sequences by taxon
record.description: Which method assigns a viral or microbial DNA sequence to the right taxon or lineage, including when it is unlike anything in the reference?

attributes.question: Which method assigns a viral or microbial DNA sequence to the right taxon or lineage, including when it is unlike anything in the reference?
intended_users: Virologists assigning taxonomy or lineage to new viral sequences
Researchers classifying sequences from a metagenomic survey
attributes.decision: Choose a classifier, and decide whether a language model's embedding adds anything over an alignment search.
inputs: Sequences to classify, with their length
The reference database and its version
Whether the taxa of interest are in the reference
attributes.output: Classification accuracy or F1 at each taxonomic level, with an alignment baseline on the same sequences where one was run.
attributes.setting: Research virology and metagenomics. Clinical pathogen identification from patient samples has its own use cases.
exclusions: Clinical DNA and RNA pathogen detection from patient samples, which have their own use cases
Metagenome assembly and binning
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from two studies: Bůžková et al. 2026's RVDB viral classification, which also compares the best embedding with BLAST, and GenBench's species and SARS-CoV-2 variant tasks. Neither holds out whole genera, so classifying sequences unlike anything in the reference is not tested.
In the BLAST comparison the embedding side is the best configuration from the 33-class test, so the same result appears in both tests.
ViroBench, which does hold out genera and deposit dates, is held while a question about one of its sources is open. CAMI's results have not passed review.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.
